cards.front: Short note: Classification of antimalarial drugs by stage of action

points: Liver stages (pre-erythrocytic, and exo-erythrocytic for P. vivax)
Blood stage (erythrocytic schizogony)
Gametocytes
Causal prophylactics: act on the pre-erythrocytic stage
Tissue schizontocides: act on liver forms, including vivax and ovale hypnozoites
Erythrocytic schizontocides: end the attack; used for clinical cure and suppressive prophylaxis
Gametocides: kill gametes and reduce mosquito transmission
Primaquine: causal prophylactic, tissue schizontocide and gametocide
Artemisinins: fastest blood schizontocides, but weak on mature gametes
Chloroquine: blood schizontocide with no liver-stage action

cards.front: Cloze: four aims of antimalarial therapy
cards.text: Antimalarial therapy aims at {{prophylaxis}} against clinical attacks, {{clinical cure}} of an attack, {{radical cure}} to remove all parasites from the body, and {{gametocidal}} action to cut transmission to mosquitoes.

cards.front: Cloze: why a blood schizontocide alone can leave relapse in vivax malaria
cards.text: P. vivax and P. ovale leave {{hypnozoites}} in the liver, so a blood schizontocide alone is followed by {{relapse}}. In falciparum malaria no such tissue stage persists, so clearing the blood adequately is a radical cure.

cards.front: Why are proguanil and pyrimethamine called low-efficacy clinical curatives?
cards.back: They are slow-acting blood schizontocides, too slow to be used alone in a non-immune patient, and parasites quickly develop resistance to them. They are therefore used only in combination, for example sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, for clinical cure.

cards.front: Essay: Chemoprophylaxis of malaria

points: Non-immune travellers and non-immune residents on fixed postings
Infants, children and pregnant women
Falciparum malaria carries serious risk in pregnancy
Short-term use in special risk groups
Choose the drug according to local resistance
Start before travel so that tolerance can be checked
Chloroquine: only where P. falciparum is still sensitive; no longer used in India
Mefloquine: weekly, for chloroquine-resistant areas; not for residents
Doxycycline: daily, for short trips; avoid in pregnancy and under 8 years
Atovaquone with proguanil: daily, used by western travellers
Proguanil with chloroquine: weekly, gives moderate protection against resistant falciparum
Primaquine protects against all species, but is not used in mass programmes because of its toxicity
Artemisinins: widespread prophylactic use would drive resistance
Proguanil alone: weak liver-stage action and rapid resistance

cards.front: How does chloroquine kill the malaria parasite inside the red cell?
cards.back: As a weak base it concentrates in the parasite's acidic food vacuole and raises its pH, which interferes with haemoglobin digestion. It also blocks conversion of toxic haem into inert haemozoin, so free haem or the haem-drug complex damages the parasite membrane.

cards.front: What is the main mechanism of chloroquine resistance in P. falciparum?
cards.back: A mutant transporter (encoded by the pfcrt gene) in the membrane of the acidic vacuole pumps chloroquine out, so less drug reaches haem. The P-glycoprotein encoded by pfmdr1 contributes and also reduces the activity of quinine and mefloquine.

cards.front: Short note: Adverse effects of chloroquine

points: Nausea, vomiting, anorexia and epigastric discomfort
Intense itching, which is the most frequent complaint
Headache and difficulty in accommodation
Retinal damage with loss of vision (seen with long courses for rheumatoid arthritis or lupus)
Corneal deposits, which are reversible on stopping
Myopathy, hearing loss, rashes, photoallergy, mood change, greying of hair
Liver damage, severe GI, neurological, retinal or blood disorders
Can precipitate seizures, porphyria and psoriasis
Must not be combined with mefloquine, amiodarone or other antiarrhythmics
Usable for treating malaria; no abortifacient or teratogenic effect reported

cards.front: Cloze: pharmacokinetics of chloroquine
cards.text: Chloroquine binds {{tightly}} to melanin and nuclear chromatin, so it concentrates in the {{liver, spleen, kidney and lungs}} and in the {{retina}}. Its terminal half-life can extend to {{1-2 months}}.

cards.front: Short note: Mefloquine

points: Effective against chloroquine-resistant falciparum
Used with artesunate as an ACT, though this combination is now less favoured
Weekly prophylaxis for travellers to multidrug-resistant areas, not for residents
GI upset, dizziness, sinus bradycardia and QT prolongation
Neuropsychiatric effects: loss of balance, ataxia, anxiety, hallucinations, rarely convulsions
Convulsions are more likely in patients recovering from cerebral malaria
Anxiety, depression, psychosis, neuropsychiatric illness or convulsions
Cardiac conduction defects or heart disease
Avoid in the first trimester unless essential
Do not give quinine, quinidine, halofantrine or chloroquine within 12 hours of a dose (QT risk)
Cannot be given parenterally; not used in severe malaria

cards.front: Short note: Quinine, uses and toxicity

points: Oldest antimalarial still in use; used when an ACT is unsuitable
Oral quinine (with doxycycline or clindamycin) for resistant falciparum
Drug of choice in the first trimester of pregnancy, with clindamycin
Tinnitus, nausea, vomiting, headache, confusion, vertigo, hearing and visual disturbance
Caused by a single large dose or several days of therapeutic doses; resolves on stopping
Rapid i.v. injection: hypotension and cardiac arrhythmia
Hypoglycaemia from insulin release; watch glucose, especially with i.v. infusion
Haemolysis with haemoglobinuria (blackwater fever), in pregnancy or falciparum infection
Single dose of about 8-10 g may be fatal
Narrow therapeutic index and a 7-day course make it less convenient than an ACT

cards.front: Which drug gives radical cure of vivax malaria, what dose, and what must be checked first?
cards.back: Primaquine, given with a full curative dose of chloroquine (or another blood schizontocide). KDT (Indian programme): 15 mg (0.25 mg/kg) daily for 14 days. GG14 (US CDC regimen): 30 mg base (0.5 mg/kg) daily for 14 days. Test for G6PD deficiency before starting, and give it with food to reduce GI upset.

cards.front: Short note: Primaquine toxicity and G6PD deficiency

points: Dose-related haemolysis
Methaemoglobinaemia, with tachypnoea and cyanosis
Its reactive metabolites are more oxidant than the parent drug
Highly susceptible patients can develop haemolytic anaemia at 15-30 mg daily
Variants differ in severity; the Mediterranean variant causes massive haemolysis
Spot tests can detect deficiency; stop the drug if dark urine appears
Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE and acute illness raise the risk
Leucopenia can occur with larger doses
Avoid, because the foetus may also be G6PD deficient
Abdominal pain, GI upset, weakness and chest discomfort; fewer with meals

cards.front: What single primaquine dose is given after falciparum treatment to reduce transmission, and where do national and WHO guidance differ?
cards.back: A single gametocidal dose given with the ACT for falciparum malaria. The Indian national programme in KDT uses 0.75 mg/kg (45 mg in adults) on day 2. WHO recommends a lower single dose of 0.25 mg/kg, and GG14 notes that at this dose G6PD testing is not required; it is given to non-pregnant patients older than 6 months in low-transmission areas. It is added even when an artemisinin is used, because artemisinins do not kill mature gametocytes.

cards.front: Cloze: tafenoquine
cards.text: Tafenoquine is a long-acting {{8-aminoquinoline}} derived from primaquine, with an elimination half-life of about {{14 days}} (primaquine: 6 to 8 hours). KDT describes it as awaiting approval; GG14 states it is now {{FDA-approved}} for malaria prophylaxis and for radical cure of P. vivax, where a {{single 300 mg dose}} is given with the blood-stage drug. It shares the risk of {{haemolysis in G6PD deficiency}}, so it is contraindicated when G6PD status is deficient or unknown and in pregnancy.

cards.front: Cloze: how primaquine differs from other antimalarials
cards.text: Primaquine is a poor {{blood}} schizontocide, but it is highly active against {{hypnozoites}} of P. vivax and ovale, against {{gametocytes}} of all species, and against the {{pre-erythrocytic}} stage of P. falciparum.

cards.front: How do artemisinins act on the parasite?
cards.back: Their endoperoxide bridge is cleaved by iron derived from haem, releasing free radicals that damage parasite membranes and proteins. A parasite calcium pump (PfATP6) is also reported to be inactivated. The result is rapid killing across ring to early schizont stages.

cards.front: Cloze: artemisinin derivatives by route
cards.text: {{Artesunate}} is water soluble and can be given orally, i.m. or {{i.v.}}. {{Artemether}} is lipid soluble and given orally or i.m., not i.v. {{Arteether}} is an i.m. oil injection for adults only. {{Arterolane}} is an oral synthetic trioxolane, used only with a partner drug.

cards.front: Why must an artemisinin never be given alone for uncomplicated falciparum malaria?
cards.back: It is short-acting, so recrudescence is common: about 50% after a 3-day course alone. A long-acting partner with a different mechanism clears the remaining parasites and prevents resistance. Monotherapy with oral artemisinins is prohibited in India.

cards.front: Artemether-lumefantrine: why must it be taken with fatty food, and what are its key interactions?
cards.back: Lumefantrine is highly lipophilic, and its absorption is poor without fat; inadequate absorption can lead to recrudescence. It inhibits CYP2D6, so drugs such as metoprolol, neuroleptics and tricyclics are affected, and it should not be given with other QT-prolonging drugs. Avoid it in the first trimester and during breastfeeding.

cards.front: Essay: Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) for uncomplicated falciparum malaria

points: The artemisinin kills more than 95% of parasites quickly, which leaves little biomass for resistance to select
The partner drug's longer action clears the remaining parasites
Each component protects the other from resistance
Rapid clinical and parasitological cure
High cure rate with low recrudescence
Good tolerability
Partner half-life matters: a long half-life allows a short course but risks subinhibitory levels that select resistant parasites
Short-acting partners need about 7 days of therapy
Artemether-lumefantrine: used in north-east India under the national programme
Artesunate with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine: first line in most of India
Artesunate-amodiaquine, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, arterolane-piperaquine; artesunate-mefloquine is less favoured
Not for severe malaria, where parenteral artemisinins are used
Not for prophylaxis
In pregnancy, preferred in the 2nd and 3rd trimester; first-trimester safety unproven

cards.front: What is the chapter's regimen for uncomplicated chloroquine-sensitive vivax malaria?
cards.back: Chloroquine 600 mg base, then 300 mg after 8 hours, then 300 mg daily for 2 more days (about 25 mg/kg over 3 days), plus primaquine 15 mg daily for 14 days. For chloroquine-resistant vivax, use quinine with doxycycline or clindamycin for 7 days (or an ACT other than artesunate-sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine), followed by primaquine.

cards.front: Chloroquine-resistant falciparum malaria in India: which regimens does the chapter list?
cards.back: The national programme treats all P. falciparum cases with an ACT, plus a single primaquine dose of 0.75 mg/kg on day 2. Options: artesunate with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (first line, except north-east India); artemether-lumefantrine (north-east India); artesunate-mefloquine; artesunate-amodiaquine; dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine; arterolane-piperaquine. Non-ACT option: quinine with doxycycline or clindamycin for 7 days.

cards.front: Severe falciparum malaria: first-choice regimen and when to switch to oral therapy
cards.back: Artesunate i.v. or i.m. 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 hours, then once daily for 7 days, switching to a 3-day oral ACT as soon as the patient can take tablets. WHO (2015) uses 3 mg/kg for children under 20 kg (KDT). Alternatives are i.m. artemether or i.m. arteether (adults) and i.v. quinine; chloroquine i.v. is a last resort in adults. GG14 notes that parenteral artesunate has now replaced quinine and quinidine for severe malaria and was FDA-approved for this in 2020.

cards.front: Short note: Falciparum malaria in pregnancy

points: Serious risk to both mother and foetus; treat promptly and aggressively
Quinine with clindamycin for 7 days; the safer option in the first trimester
Safety of artemisinins in the first trimester is unproven
A 3-day ACT is preferred over the 7-day quinine course
Intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine in high-transmission areas
Treat with chloroquine as in non-pregnant patients
Defer radical cure with primaquine until after delivery
Primaquine, because the foetus may be G6PD deficient
Doxycycline, which is contraindicated in pregnancy

cards.front: What is the role of doxycycline and clindamycin in malaria?
cards.back: Both are slow-acting schizontocides with no useful effect on liver stages or gametocytes. They are never used alone for malaria; they are added to quinine or an artemisinin to potentiate it. Doxycycline is a second-line prophylactic for short trips to chloroquine-resistant areas, but is not used in children or pregnancy. Clindamycin can be used in children and pregnancy.

cards.front: How does metronidazole kill anaerobic protozoa and bacteria?
cards.back: It diffuses into the organism, where anaerobic electron-transport proteins reduce its nitro group to a reactive nitro radical. The radical damages cell components and competes for electrons from the pyruvate-ferredoxin pathway, disrupting energy metabolism. Oxygen blocks this activation, which is why aerobic organisms are spared.

cards.front: Short note: Metronidazole, uses and adverse effects

points: First line for all forms of amoebiasis
Giardiasis and trichomoniasis
Anaerobic infections, including post-surgical and brain abscess
C. difficile colitis: KDT lists it, but GG14 states that oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin are now preferred, with metronidazole only for non-severe disease
H. pylori eradication in triple therapy; ANUG
Anorexia, nausea, metallic taste and abdominal cramps
Headache, glossitis and dry mouth
Allergic urticaria or fixed drug eruption: stop, and avoid all nitroimidazoles afterwards
Peripheral neuropathy and CNS effects with prolonged use; seizures at very high doses
Leucopenia with repeated courses
Thrombophlebitis if the i.v. solution is not well diluted
Neurological disease, blood dyscrasias and first trimester
Use with caution in chronic alcoholics
Potentiates warfarin by blocking its metabolism
Reduces lithium clearance, risking toxicity
Enzyme inducers reduce its effect

cards.front: Cloze: metronidazole and alcohol
cards.text: Some patients taking metronidazole develop a {{disulfiram-like}} reaction when they drink {{alcohol}}, but most patients can drink without reaction. Because of this, alcohol is avoided during treatment and for a period afterwards.

cards.front: Cloze: tinidazole compared with metronidazole
cards.text: Tinidazole has a half-life of about {{12 hours}}, so it suits {{single-dose or once-daily}} regimens. It is {{equally efficacious}} but has {{fewer}} side effects than metronidazole.

cards.front: What is the role of diloxanide furoate in amoebiasis?
cards.back: It is a luminal amoebicide that kills intestinal trophozoites which would otherwise form cysts. The ester is hydrolysed in the gut and the released diloxanide is absorbed, but it has no useful systemic amoebicidal action. It is the preferred drug for mild intestinal disease and asymptomatic cyst passers, given with or after a tissue amoebicide, with 80-90% cure in mild disease.

cards.front: Why are emetine and dehydroemetine now restricted in amoebiasis?
cards.back: They are potent direct tissue amoebicides, but they must be given by injection because they cause vomiting. Cardiotoxicity (ECG changes, myocarditis, hypotension) and cumulative toxicity limit their use. They are reserved for patients who cannot take metronidazole, for no more than about 10 days, and a luminal amoebicide must always follow. Dehydroemetine is preferred because it is less cardiotoxic.

cards.front: Cloze: chloroquine in amoebiasis
cards.text: Chloroquine kills {{trophozoites}} and is concentrated in the {{liver}}, so it is used only for {{hepatic amoebiasis}}. It does not clear the intestinal cyst reservoir, so a {{luminal amoebicide}} must always follow.

cards.front: Essay: Amoebic liver abscess

points: Trophozoites reach the liver via the portal vein from an intestinal focus
Fever, right upper quadrant pain and hepatomegaly; ultrasound shows the abscess, and stool may be negative
Metronidazole 800 mg TDS for 10 days (i.v. 500 mg 6-hourly in severe cases) followed by oral therapy
Tinidazole 2 g daily for 3-6 days; i.v. tinidazole in severe cases
Dehydroemetine, only if metronidazole cannot be used or fails
Chloroquine after a nitroimidazole or emetine, if response is incomplete
Large abscesses can take months to resolve even after trophozoites are killed
Aspiration may be needed for a large abscess
Give a luminal amoebicide to clear the intestinal reservoir and prevent a carrier state

cards.front: Why were 8-hydroxyquinolines withdrawn in some countries?
cards.back: Prolonged, high-dose quiniodochlor caused an epidemic of subacute myelo-optic neuropathy (SMON) in Japan in the 1970s, and other members caused neuropathy and visual impairment. They were banned in Japan and some other countries. In India their use is prohibited in children, because chronic use has caused blindness.

cards.front: Cloze: drugs for giardiasis
cards.text: {{Metronidazole}} 400 mg TDS for 5-7 days, {{tinidazole}} as a 2 g single dose, or {{secnidazole}} as a 2 g single dose are first-choice options. {{Nitazoxanide}} 500 mg BD for 3 days is an alternative, and about {{10%}} of patients may need a second course.

cards.front: Trichomoniasis: first-choice oral drugs and how to prevent reinfection
cards.back: Metronidazole 2 g as a single dose (or 400 mg TDS for 7 days), tinidazole, or secnidazole 2 g single dose. Recurrence is common; repeat a course after 4-6 weeks if needed. Treat the male partner at the same time to prevent reinfection. Intravaginal agents are reserved for refractory cases.

cards.front: Which drug is first line for visceral leishmaniasis in India now, and why is sodium stibogluconate no longer used?
cards.back: Oral miltefosine is the first-line drug under the national programme. Leishmania donovani in Bihar and nearby areas is resistant to sodium stibogluconate (SSG); over 60% of cases in Bihar did not respond, so SSG is no longer used in India.

cards.front: Miltefosine: dosing, key adverse effects and pregnancy warning
cards.back: Given orally with meals for 28 days. Under the national programme (KDT): 100 mg daily for adults over 25 kg, 50 mg daily for those under 25 kg, and 2.5 mg/kg daily for children aged 2-11. Common effects are anorexia, vomiting and diarrhoea; transaminase rise and renal dysfunction are usually reversible. It is teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy. Contraception is needed during treatment and afterwards: KDT gives 3 months, while GG14 notes that US guidance requires 5 months, in keeping with its long half-life (1 to 4 weeks).

cards.front: Cloze: drug options for visceral leishmaniasis
cards.text: {{Miltefosine}} is the first-line oral drug in India. {{Amphotericin B deoxycholate}} is the second-line drug under the national programme, while WHO prefers {{liposomal amphotericin B}}. {{Paromomycin}} given i.m. for 21 days is an alternative, and {{sodium stibogluconate}} is used only where the parasite is still sensitive.

cards.front: How does amphotericin B act on Leishmania, and why is it the drug of choice in pregnancy?
cards.back: Leishmania, like fungi, has ergosterol in its membrane, and amphotericin B binds ergosterol to damage the membrane. It is the preferred drug in pregnant and breastfeeding women because miltefosine is teratogenic.

cards.front: Short note: Treatment of visceral leishmaniasis

points: Miltefosine: oral, 28 days, first line in India
Amphotericin B deoxycholate: 0.75-1 mg/kg on alternate days to 15 mg/kg total; second line in India
Liposomal amphotericin B: 3-5 mg/kg daily for 3-5 days (total 15 mg/kg); WHO first preference, with a single 10 mg/kg option
Paromomycin: 15 mg/kg daily i.m. for 21 days
Sodium stibogluconate: 20 mg Sb/kg for 30 days, only where the parasite is still sensitive
Liposomal amphotericin 5 mg/kg single dose plus miltefosine for 7 days
Liposomal amphotericin 5 mg/kg single dose plus paromomycin for 10 days
Miltefosine plus paromomycin, each for 10 days; cure about 98-99%
Failures are treated with higher doses of amphotericin B or liposomal amphotericin B
Cure: clinical improvement with no relapse for 6 months; spleen aspirate negative
Poorer response to both antileishmanial and anti-HIV drugs and higher mortality; intensive therapy needed
Local sodium stibogluconate or 15% paromomycin ointment for small dermal lesions; systemic drugs for multiple or severe lesions

cards.front: How does mebendazole kill intestinal worms?
cards.back: It binds the parasite's beta-tubulin with high affinity and blocks microtubule formation, which also reduces glucose uptake and glycogen stores. Worms are immobilised and die slowly, over 2-3 days, and hatching of nematode eggs is inhibited. It is poorly absorbed, so it acts in the gut.

cards.front: Cloze: albendazole pharmacokinetics
cards.text: Albendazole is converted by first-pass metabolism to an active {{sulfoxide}} metabolite, which is widely distributed and enters the {{brain}}. Absorption is improved by a {{fatty}} meal, which is why it is given with food for cysticercosis and hydatid disease.

cards.front: Cloze: first-choice anthelmintic for selected worms
cards.text: Strongyloides: {{ivermectin}}. Trichuris: {{mebendazole}}. Trichinella and hydatid disease: {{albendazole}}. Tapeworms (Taenia, Hymenolepis): {{praziquantel}}. Wuchereria and Brugia: {{diethylcarbamazine}} or ivermectin; GG14 notes that a single dose of the triple combination {{ivermectin + DEC + albendazole}} is highly effective in lymphatic filariasis.

cards.front: Pyrantel: mechanism, and why it should not be combined with piperazine
cards.back: Pyrantel activates nicotinic receptors on worm muscle, causing persistent depolarisation that leads to slow spastic paralysis and expulsion. Piperazine has the opposite effect, hyperpolarising worm muscle, so it antagonises pyrantel and the two should not be used together.

cards.front: Piperazine: mechanism and contraindications
cards.back: It acts as a GABA agonist on Ascaris muscle, opening chloride channels. This hyperpolarises the muscle, producing flaccid paralysis, so worms are expelled alive. It is contraindicated in renal insufficiency and epilepsy, and is considered safe in pregnancy.

cards.front: Levamisole: current role in helminthiasis
cards.back: It is a second-line anthelmintic restricted to ascariasis and ancylostomiasis (hookworm). It stimulates worm ganglia, causing tonic paralysis and expulsion of live worms. Its immunomodulatory use in other diseases has been abandoned because repeated doses cause severe reactions.

cards.front: Diethylcarbamazine: which filarial stages does it kill?
cards.back: It is highly selective for microfilariae and clears them from blood within about a week, but does not clear those in nodules or fluid collections. Prolonged courses slowly kill adult worms, so it is repeated to achieve a radical cure. It is also used in tropical pulmonary eosinophilia.

cards.front: Diethylcarbamazine: how is the febrile reaction reduced?
cards.back: Mass death of microfilariae and adult worms causes fever, rash, itching, lymphadenopathy, bronchospasm and fall in blood pressure. Start with a low dose and build up to the full dose over a few days; if a reaction occurs, hold DEC and give an antihistamine or corticosteroid (GG14: such pretreatment is often used). In loiasis and onchocerciasis reactions can be life-threatening: KDT advises a small test dose or initial ivermectin. GG14 states that DEC is contraindicated in onchocerciasis (it worsens eye lesions), ivermectin being preferred, and that ivermectin can itself cause encephalopathy in patients with very heavy Loa loa microfilaraemia.

cards.front: Ivermectin: mechanism and main indications
cards.back: It opens invertebrate glutamate-gated chloride channels, paralysing nematodes; it also kills scabies mites and lice. It poorly enters the mammalian CNS because of P-glycoprotein efflux. Key uses: onchocerciasis (repeated doses every 6-12 months), strongyloidiasis, scabies, pediculosis and cutaneous larva migrans. It is microfilaricidal but not macrofilaricidal.

cards.front: Praziquantel: mechanism and spectrum
cards.back: It causes calcium leakage in susceptible worms, producing contracture and paralysis; at higher concentrations it vacuolates the tegument, so the host's immunity destroys the worm. It acts on schistosomes, most flukes and cestodes (adult and larval stages), but not on nematodes.

cards.front: Short note: Niclosamide and the Taenia solium precaution

points: Blocks oxidative phosphorylation in the tapeworm, which is then partly digested in the gut
Poorly absorbed, so little systemic toxicity; tasteless
After a light breakfast: 2 g chewed over one day (2 tablets, then 2 more an hour later)
Saline purge 2 hours after the last dose
Search the stool for the scolex to confirm expulsion
Digestion of T. solium segments can release eggs that develop into larvae and cause visceral cysticercosis
A thorough purge is needed; praziquantel is preferred for T. solium
H. nana: 2 g daily for 5 days, as the cysticerci of H. nana are not affected in one dose

cards.front: Essay: Management of neurocysticercosis

points: Treat active cysts, multiple parenchymal cysts, and intraventricular cysts likely to cause hydrocephalus
Inactive or calcified cysts may be left alone
Seizures are controlled symptomatically in all cases
Albendazole is preferred: shorter course (8-15 days), cure of 75-85% against 50-60% for praziquantel, and cheaper
Praziquantel, 50 mg/kg daily in 3 divided doses for 15-30 days, is the second choice
Phenytoin and carbamazepine lower praziquantel levels, so a higher dose may be needed
Corticosteroids raise albendazole absorption but lower praziquantel levels
Start a corticosteroid 2 days before and continue for 2 weeks after the anthelmintic course
Start an anticonvulsant before the anthelmintic and continue for 1-6 months after it
Do not give an anthelmintic for ocular cysticercosis: the reaction can cause blindness
Intraventricular or subarachnoid cysts may need a month or longer of treatment
Expelling the adult tapeworm from the gut removes the source of future cysts

cards.front: Why is albendazole preferred over praziquantel for neurocysticercosis?
cards.back: It needs a shorter course (8-15 days, against 15-30 days for praziquantel), gives higher cure rates in symptom resolution and cyst disappearance (75-85% against 50-60%), and is cheaper. Praziquantel is therefore the second choice.

cards.front: Hydatid disease: albendazole regimen and its role around surgery
cards.back: KDT: 400 mg twice daily for 4 weeks, repeated after 2 weeks if needed, for up to 3 courses; mebendazole is less effective. GG14 calls albendazole the drug of choice for cystic hydatid disease: prolonged treatment gives only modest cure, but it is used around surgery or cyst puncture-aspiration to reduce the risk of dissemination from spilled cyst contents, and for inoperable cysts. Monitor liver function and blood counts on repeated courses.

cards.front: Moxidectin: how does it compare with ivermectin?
cards.back: A macrocyclic lactone related to ivermectin and FDA-approved for onchocerciasis, where it is more active than ivermectin. Unlike ivermectin it is a poor P-glycoprotein substrate. It has a very long elimination half-life (about 23 days in onchocerciasis) and is given as a single 8 mg oral dose. Mazzotti-type reactions (itching, rash, tachycardia, fall in blood pressure) are common after treatment. It has not been used in children under 12 years. It also shows activity in strongyloidiasis and, with albendazole, in trichuriasis.

cards.front: Short note: Recent advances in malaria treatment

points: Artemisinin 'resistance' is delayed parasite clearance over hours, linked to kelch13 mutations
Partner-drug resistance (e.g. piperaquine) makes ACT failure substantial
Recrudescence exceeds 50% in parts of Asia
Triple ACT (artemisinin plus two partners) is being tested
Parenteral artesunate FDA-approved in 2020 for severe falciparum malaria
Tafenoquine: long-acting 8-aminoquinoline, FDA-approved for uses similar to primaquine
Pyronaridine-artesunate: effective against P. falciparum and P. vivax; not FDA-licensed but available globally
ACT not recommended in the first trimester or for children weighing 5 kg or less
Artemether-lumefantrine first-trimester data may widen ACT use in pregnancy
